name: Carlos Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a first-year lineworker on a crew that covers the mountain roads around Alto Ridge, so a lot of it is keeping power going to ski villages and farms up the passes. When it's quiet we replace old poles and insulators, and when it snows we're out restoring lines at all hours. I'm the slowest climber on the crew, no question, but I'm getting better. Before this I worked in a warehouse that went half robot in two years, which is partly why I wanted a job with my hands up a pole.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Driving more than climbing, honestly, hours on switchback roads in the crew truck. And money, I'm still paying off a car loan from my warehouse days and I've got about a week of savings. On weekends I fix e-bikes for tourists out of my roommate Felix's garage, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the hype was always bigger than the thing. I'd probably post something like, still need a human to climb in a blizzard. Then I'd keep using it for the boring stuff, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a decent outcome for me. I use AI every day, to study, to plan e-bike repairs, to argue with my bank, and that'd keep going. My job stays solid, and I'd have time to grow the bike thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, keep my head down on the crew, and push the e-bike side harder, maybe rent a proper corner of a garage next summer. I'd use AI to sort out pricing and a booking page, because I'm bad at that stuff. Pay off the car first, then save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a bit flat. I like the idea of big change, but I won't miss the stress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the warehouse went half robot. What was that like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weird, mostly. The robots took the walking and lifting, and the people who stayed were the ones who learned to fix them or watch the screens. I left before I found out which one I'd be, but I learned that standing still is the dangerous bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the e-bike work bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two hundred a month in summer, almost nothing in winter. It's not life-changing, but it's the difference between the car payment being scary and being fine. And I like it, it's tinkering.

S0.say: He's not surprised, because the hype was always bigger than the thing, and he'd post that you still need a human to climb in a blizzard. He'd keep using AI for the boring stuff.
S0.think: It's a decent outcome: his daily AI use for study, repairs and bank arguments continues, his job stays solid, and he has time to grow his e-bike side work.
S0.do: Qualifies and pushes the e-bike business, possibly renting a garage corner next summer. Uses AI for pricing and a booking page, pays off the car loan, then starts saving.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, though he won't miss the stress.
S0.quote: I left before I found out which one I'd be, but I learned that standing still is the dangerous bit.
S0.fieldNote: His earlier warehouse job, which went half robot in two years, shapes everything he says about change. He's already building a second income from e-bike repairs, small but steadying. AI is part of his everyday life, not a novelty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's just the next step, and people who learn the tools will be fine. That's what happened at the warehouse. I'd tell my crew to try the drone and the new apps instead of moaning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think line work holds up well in this one, because the mountains are hard on machines. Ice on the lines, roads closed by landslides, no signal for half the valley. But fewer of the cushy jobs, like patrols and paperwork, would be left for juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up for every pilot programme the company runs, drones, smart meters, the fault-finding software. I'd keep growing the bike repairs, maybe add servicing for the e-scooters the resort rents out. And I'd keep using AI to study faster, so I'm qualified sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. It feels like a game I know how to play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That being keen isn't enough if they cut juniors anyway. I've got a week of savings and a car loan. If they let me go, being good with a drone won't pay the rent in Alto Ridge, where there's one line crew for an hour in any direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for how this goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody and everybody, really. Companies want to save money, governments are slow, and workers have to meet it halfway. I don't think there's a villain, it's just math.

S1.say: It's just the next step, and people who learn the tools will be fine, as at the warehouse. He'd tell his crew to try the drone and apps instead of moaning.
S1.think: Mountain line work holds up well because ice, landslides and patchy signal are hard on machines. But fewer easy jobs like patrols and paperwork would be left for juniors.
S1.do: Volunteers for every company pilot, from drones to fault-finding software. Expands his repair work to the resort's rental e-scooters and uses AI to study faster and qualify sooner.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like a game he knows how to play.
S1.quote: I don't think there's a villain, it's just math.
S1.fieldNote: He's eager and practical, volunteering for pilots where others would resist. Underneath, he knows his week of savings and the single local crew make enthusiasm a limited defence. His centrist view refuses to blame any one group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for most people and somebody has to soften the landing, maybe a temporary income while people switch. I wouldn't say stop it, because I don't think you can. I'd say get ready, now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scrambling. If robots can climb poles in ice, and AI can do the fixing, my plan to be the guy who's good with both doesn't hold for long. And with a week of savings, I don't get to wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply straight away to whichever company is rolling out the robots, as a field tech or a fleet operator, the person who drives them up the passes and pulls them out of the snow. I'd sell my car and take the bus if I had to. I'd squeeze every bit of money out of the bike repairs before robots do those too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, definitely. But I'd be moving too fast to sit with it much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change, compared with a slower version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's no time to retrain properly, so you just jump to whatever's hiring humans right now. With two years, I'd skip finishing my apprenticeship if a robot company offered me a job. It's a land grab for the last good seats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Felix, I suppose, he'd let me slide on rent for a month. My parents are in the city and they're not rich, my dad's a bus driver, so he's probably in the same boat. I'd try not to need anyone, but I'm not daft.

S2.say: It's too fast for most people, and someone needs to soften the landing, perhaps with a temporary income while people switch. He wouldn't say stop it, because he thinks it can't be stopped.
S2.think: He'd be scrambling, since robots that climb in ice plus AI that fixes would undo his plan to be good at both. With a week of savings he can't wait and see.
S2.do: Applies immediately to robot rollout companies as a field technician or fleet operator, even leaving his apprenticeship. Sells his car if needed and squeezes all he can from bike repairs.
S2.feel: Anxious, but moving too fast to dwell on it.
S2.quote: It's a land grab for the last good seats.
S2.fieldNote: Two years turns his adaptability into a scramble: he'd abandon his apprenticeship for a robot company job. His week of savings is the real constraint. He's realistic that his support network is thin, with parents in a similar position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a plan, so make one. Talk to the company, find out what training they'll pay for, and don't wait for someone to hand you a leaflet. I'd say that to the guys on the crew who are older than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means I can actually finish my apprenticeship and add robot skills on top. I'd be one of the few people who knows the lines and the machines. I don't know how long that lasts after 2031, but it'd buy me some good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify in three years, using AI to speed up the study, then do a robotics maintenance course online, nights. I'd pay off the car and start saving properly, maybe a hundred a month. And I'd keep the bike side going, it's my backup plan, small as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd have a plan, but I'd know it's a plan with an expiry date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for over those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the first robot actually climbs a pole in Alto Ridge, not in a video. Videos always look perfect. Up here, the first robot that slides off an iced pole will tell me how much time I've really got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the plan has an expiry date. What comes after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I genuinely don't know, and I don't think anyone does. Maybe I'd have some savings and the bike thing and I'd be okay for a while. I'm good at jumping, but at some point there's nowhere left to jump.

S3.say: Five years is enough to make a plan, so people should ask the company what training it will fund rather than wait for a leaflet. He'd say that to older crewmates.
S3.think: He can finish his apprenticeship and add robot skills, becoming one of the few who know both lines and machines. He doesn't know how long that lasts after 2031, but it would buy some good years.
S3.do: Qualifies in three years with AI-assisted study, then takes an online robotics maintenance course at night. Pays off the car, saves about a hundred a month and keeps the bike repairs as a backup.
S3.feel: Uneasy, holding a plan he knows has an expiry date.
S3.quote: I'm good at jumping, but at some point there's nowhere left to jump.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns his scramble into a deliberate bridge between line work and robotics. He's clear-eyed that this only buys time. His test for the timeline is a robot coping with an iced pole in his own valley, not a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and anyone who's caught out by 2036 wasn't paying attention. But I'd also say the government should help people who can't retrain easily. Not everyone's twenty-seven with nothing to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's honestly not bad. I'd get proper years on the lines, build skills, maybe build up the bike business into something real. The question is what any of us do once it arrives, and I don't have an answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, qualify and keep the routine, then buy a proper diagnostic kit for e-bikes, maybe four hundred, and start a real little shop. I'd use AI to track which skills are still in demand every year. In five or six years, I'd decide between robotics and the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mild. More curious than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years let you do that five doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build something that's mine, slowly, instead of just chasing the next job. In five years I'm a lineworker who knows robots. In ten, I could be a guy with a small business, and businesses can own robots too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not everyone's twenty-seven with nothing to lose. Who were you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta on our crew, she's fifty-four and climbs better than me but hates screens. Ten years puts her at sixty-four, which is too early to stop and too late to start. People like her need real help, not a speech about adapting.

S4.say: Ten years is a long runway and anyone caught out by 2036 wasn't paying attention, but the government should help those who can't retrain easily. Not everyone is twenty-seven with nothing to lose.
S4.think: It's not bad for him: proper years on the lines and time to turn the bike work into something real. He has no answer for what anyone does once it arrives.
S4.do: Qualifies and keeps his routine, then buys a diagnostic kit of about four hundred to start a small e-bike shop. Uses AI yearly to track in-demand skills and decides between robotics and the shop in five or six years.
S4.feel: Mildly uneasy, more curious than scared.
S4.quote: In ten, I could be a guy with a small business, and businesses can own robots too.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years his thinking moves from jobs to ownership: a small business that could own robots. He still admits he has no answer for after it arrives. His concern for older colleague Marta softens his earlier line that it's just math.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to jump with a week of savings and no time to land properly. What would help is a few months of income while people switch, and companies that bring in robots having to train their own workers first. That way people like me could get a seat without starving for it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the robots breaking. Somebody has to fix them, drive them up the mountain and drag them out of the snow. I'd like to know if that's a real job or just a short one.

headlineQuote: Somebody has to fix them, drive them up the mountain and drag them out of the snow.
portrait: Carlos Abbott is a 27-year-old first-year lineworker on a mountain crew, the slowest climber in the team, who left a warehouse after watching it go half robot in two years. He uses AI every day, fixes e-bikes for tourists on weekends for about two hundred a month in summer, and is paying off a car loan with a week of savings. He's calm through the plateau and steady change, volunteering for every new tool, and anxious but racing for a robot-company job if AGI arrives in two years. With five or ten years he plans a bridge into robotics or his own small shop, while admitting no plan survives the end point. He blames no one, but softens when he thinks of older colleagues like Marta.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd have to jump with a week of savings and no time to land properly.
whatWouldHelp: A few months of income while people switch jobs, and a rule that companies bringing in robots train their own workers first.
